history.heading: Silk Road cities
paragraphs: Uzbekistan, in the heart of Central Asia, was home to ancient civilisations such as Sogdiana, Bactria and Khwarezm. Its cities, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, became great centres of trade and learning on the Silk Road. Alexander the Great conquered the region in the 4th century BCE.

Arab armies brought Islam in the 8th century. Scholars such as al-Khwarizmi (from whose name the word "algorithm" derives), al-Biruni, Avicenna and Imam al-Bukhari came from the region. Genghis Khan devastated it in 1220. In the 14th century Timur (Tamerlane) built an empire from Samarkand, whose Registan square and Bibi-Khanym Mosque are masterpieces. His grandson Ulugh Beg built a famous observatory.

history.heading: Khanates and Russian rule
paragraphs: From the 16th century, the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand ruled the region. The Russian Empire conquered them in the 1860s and 1870s. The Uzbek SSR was created in 1924. Soviet policies expanded cotton monoculture, which drained the rivers feeding the Aral Sea, causing it to shrink dramatically.

Uzbekistan became independent on 1 September 1991. Islam Karimov ruled with an iron fist until his death in 2016; security forces killed hundreds of protesters in Andijan in 2005. His successor, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, has opened up the economy and improved regional relations.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Uzbek, a Turkic language now written in Latin script, is the official language; Russian and Tajik are also spoken. Most people are Sunni Muslim. The historic centres of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Plov, rice cooked with meat, carrots and spices, is the national dish and recognised by UNESCO. Uzbek crafts include suzani embroidery, ikat silk and ceramics. Shashmaqam music and Navruz celebrations are important.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Uzbekistan is a presidential republic in which the president holds strong powers. A 2023 constitutional referendum extended presidential terms to seven years and reset Mirziyoyev's term count. Reforms have reduced forced labour in cotton fields and eased some restrictions, but political opposition remains limited.

economy.heading: Opening up
paragraphs: Uzbekistan has the largest population in Central Asia. Its economy relies on natural gas, gold (it is one of the world's largest producers), copper, cotton, textiles and agriculture. Remittances from workers in Russia are important. Since 2017 currency liberalisation and reforms have attracted investment and tourism. The currency is the som.
